TGD4-Reciprocating-Compressors-11.question: How is the methane reduction from replacing reciprocating compressor rod packing determined?
TGD4-Reciprocating-Compressors-11.answer: By the difference between the leak rate measured before packing replacement and the emissions measured from the newly installed packing.
TGD4-Reciprocating-Compressors-11.evidence: packing by the difference between measurements of leak rates prior to packing replacement and measurements of emissions from newly installed packing

TGD4-Reciprocating-Compressors-11.question: What costs should be included when assessing reciprocating compressor rod packing replacement economics?
TGD4-Reciprocating-Compressors-11.answer: Equipment replacement costs, the value of gas saved based on leak measurement, and the costs of any production stops needed to carry out the maintenance.
TGD4-Reciprocating-Compressors-11.evidence: Partners should include the costs associated with production stops, if such stops are required to carry out the maintenance/replacement

TGD4-Reciprocating-Compressors-11.question: What do Teflon packing ring sets and piston rods cost for reciprocating compressors?
TGD4-Reciprocating-Compressors-11.answer: A typical Teflon 8- to 10-cup ring set costs about $1,350 to $1,700, and piston rods are estimated at $2,400 to $4,700.
TGD4-Reciprocating-Compressors-11.evidence: a typical Teflon 8- to 10-cup ring set ranges from about $1,350 to $1,700. For piston rods, the replacement cost is determined by the dimension and type of rod. Partners estimate the cost of rods to range from $2,400 to $4,700.

TGD4-Reciprocating-Compressors-11.question: What are the trade-offs of tungsten carbide or chromium coatings on compressor piston rods?
TGD4-Reciprocating-Compressors-11.answer: These coatings increase the cost but extend the life of the rods and rings.
TGD4-Reciprocating-Compressors-11.evidence: Certain coatings such as tungsten carbide or chromium can increase the costs but extend the life of rods and rings as well.

TGD4-Reciprocating-Compressors-11.question: What is the economic replacement threshold for reciprocating compressor packing rings?
TGD4-Reciprocating-Compressors-11.answer: It is the leak reduction at which replacing packing rings (and rods if needed) becomes cost-effective, calculated with discounted cash flow from the replacement cost, discount factor, operating hours per year and gas price.
TGD4-Reciprocating-Compressors-11.evidence: Partners can determine an “economic replacement threshold” that will indicate when replacing packing rings (and rods, if necessary) is cost-effective

TGD4-Reciprocating-Compressors-12.question: What leak reduction pays back a reciprocating compressor packing ring replacement in one year?
TGD4-Reciprocating-Compressors-12.answer: With a $1,620 ring replacement cost plus $1,620 labor, an expected leak reduction of 4.2 scmh (148 scfh) pays back in one year.
TGD4-Reciprocating-Compressors-12.evidence: For this example, the $1,620 ring replacement cost plus $1,620 labor can be paid back in one year with an expected leak reduction of 4.2 scmh (148 scfh).

TGD4-Reciprocating-Compressors-12.question: When should packing rings be replaced if a company requires a two-year payback?
TGD4-Reciprocating-Compressors-12.answer: When the expected leak reduction is at or above the economic replacement threshold of approximately 2.2 scmh (78 scfh), because the value of gas saved then exceeds the cost.
TGD4-Reciprocating-Compressors-12.evidence: If a Partner’s internal criterion for project investment is a payback of two years, the economic replacement threshold should be approximately 2.2 scmh (78 scfh).

TGD4-Reciprocating-Compressors-12.question: What do the terms i and n mean in the discount factor for the rod packing economic replacement threshold?
TGD4-Reciprocating-Compressors-12.answer: i is the discount rate or the Partner's hurdle rate expressed as a decimal, and n is the selected payback period.
TGD4-Reciprocating-Compressors-12.evidence: Where: I = discount rate or Partner hurdle rate (expressed as a decimal). n = the payback period selected.

TGD4-Reciprocating-Compressors-14.question: Where can reciprocating compressor rod packing vent gas be routed instead of venting?
TGD4-Reciprocating-Compressors-14.answer: To useful outlets such as a fuel gas system, a VRU or a compressor inlet, or to a flare.
TGD4-Reciprocating-Compressors-14.evidence: Partners can reduce venting emissions by routing gas to useful outlets, including a fuel gas system, a VRU, or a compressor inlet.

TGD4-Reciprocating-Compressors-14.question: What must Partners check before connecting a reciprocating compressor vent line to an existing VRU?
TGD4-Reciprocating-Compressors-14.answer: The incoming gas composition and volume, and that the VRU has enough capacity for the maximum anticipated volume from the compressor vents.
TGD4-Reciprocating-Compressors-14.evidence: the Partner must ensure the VRU has sufficient capacity to accept the maximum anticipated volume from the compressor vent(s)

TGD4-Reciprocating-Compressors-14.question: How do methane reductions compare between routing rod packing gas to a VRU and to a flare?
TGD4-Reciprocating-Compressors-14.answer: Up to 95 percent with a VRU (its operating factor), and up to 99 percent with a flare connection, assuming 99 percent flare efficiency.
TGD4-Reciprocating-Compressors-14.evidence: Partners can expect to reduce methane emissions by up to 95 percent from reciprocating compressor venting when routing rod packing emission to a VRU (the operating factor of a VRU) and by up to 99 percent when implementing a flare connection (assuming 99 percent flare efficiency).

TGD4-Reciprocating-Compressors-14.question: What are the main costs of routing reciprocating compressor vent gas to an existing VRU?
TGD4-Reciprocating-Compressors-14.answer: Mainly piping and installation. Incremental O&M is negligible: routine inspection and maintenance plus extra electricity for the added VRU throughput.
TGD4-Reciprocating-Compressors-14.evidence: Assuming a facility has an existing useful outlet such as a VRU, the cost of piping and installation costs would be the main associated expenses for this opportunity.

TGD4-Reciprocating-Compressors-14.question: Why might a Partner route rod packing gas to a flare even though it gives no direct economic benefit?
TGD4-Reciprocating-Compressors-14.answer: OGMP suggests considering indirect benefits such as safety benefits and reputational risk mitigation.
TGD4-Reciprocating-Compressors-14.evidence: OGMP suggests that, when assessing this option, Partners consider the indirect benefits associated with this option (e.g., safety benefits, reputational risk mitigation).

TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-01.question: What is the purpose of a glycol dehydrator in natural gas operations?
TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-01.answer: To remove water from a wet gas stream using monoethylene glycol, diethylene glycol, or most commonly triethylene glycol (TEG).
TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-01.evidence: Glycol dehydrators in the natural gas industry have the primary purpose of removing water from an incoming wet gas stream using monoethylene glycol, diethylene glycol, or, most commonly, triethylene glycol (TEG).

TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-01.question: Why does a glycol dehydrator emit methane?
TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-01.answer: Besides water, the glycol absorbs smaller amounts of methane, VOCs and HAPs. These are boiled off with the water in the regenerator/reboiler and routed with the steam to disposal such as the atmosphere or a flare.
TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-01.evidence: In addition to the absorbed water, methane, HAPs, and VOCS are boiled off and routed with the steam to disposal (atmosphere, flare, etc.).

TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-01.question: What is stripping gas in a glycol dehydrator and how does it affect emissions?
TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-01.answer: Some dehydrators inject gas into the glycol feed to the regenerator to help remove water at a lower temperature; this gas then vents with the steam and other gases.
TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-01.evidence: Some dehydrators inject gas into the glycol feed to the regenerator to act as a “stripping gas” to aid in removing water from the glycol at a lower temperature. This gas vents with the steam and other gases.

TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-01.question: How does an energy exchange glycol pump work?
TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-01.answer: Low-pressure glycol is pumped into the absorber by pistons driven by the high-pressure glycol leaving the absorber.
TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-01.evidence: In the case of energy exchange pumps, the low-pressure glycol is pumped into the absorber by pistons driven by the high-pressure glycol leaving the absorber.

TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-01.question: Why can internal pump seal leaks make a glycol dehydrator less efficient?
TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-01.answer: Wet glycol leaking through the internal pump seals contaminates the dry glycol, so a higher circulation rate is needed to meet dry gas moisture specifications.
TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-01.evidence: the wet glycol can leak through the internal pump seals and contaminate the dry glycol, causing the dehydrator to operate less efficiently, requiring a higher circulation rate to achieve dry gas moisture specifications

TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-02.question: What does a flash tank separator do in a glycol dehydrator system?
TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-02.answer: It separates free gas, including motive gas and some dissolved gas, from the rich glycol before the regenerator, at a pressure that lets the gas be used for fuel, low-pressure sales or compressor suction.
TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-02.evidence: Additional motive gas and some of the dissolved gas can be separated from the rich glycol ahead of the regenerator with a “flash tank separator.”

TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-02.question: How effective is a glycol dehydrator flash tank with an energy exchange pump compared with an electric pump?
TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-02.answer: With an energy exchange pump, a flash tank captures approximately 90 percent of the methane entrained by the TEG; with an electric pump it achieves only small reductions.
TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-02.evidence: A flash tank captures approximately 90 percent of the methane entrained by the TEG when using an energy exchange pump, but achieves only small reductions (some of the dissolved hydrocarbons) using an electric pump.

TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-02.question: How can methane be recovered from a glycol dehydrator regenerator vent?
TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-02.answer: An air condenser on the regenerator vent condenses the steam so the non-condensable methane can be recovered.
TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-02.evidence: Putting an air condenser on the regenerator vent can condense the steam so that the noncondensable methane can be recovered.

TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-04.question: What failures can raise emissions from a mitigated glycol dehydrator system?
TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-04.answer: A venting system malfunction or an extinguished flare.
TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-04.evidence: Possible equipment failures resulting from improperly functioning systems include a venting system malfunction or an extinguished flare.

TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-04.question: What should Partners evaluate when glycol dehydrator gases are routed to a flare?
TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-04.answer: The flow rate and composition of the gases sent to the flare, to estimate the methane emissions that result from the flare's combustion efficiency.
TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-04.evidence: Partners should evaluate gases from glycol dehydrator that are routed to a flare (flow rate, composition) to estimate methane emissions resulting from the flare combustion efficiency.

TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-05.question: Which quantification methods does the OGMP recommend for glycol dehydrator methane emissions?
TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-05.answer: Direct measurement, engineering calculation with software, or emission factor calculation. Direct measurement is in principle the most accurate.
TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-05.evidence: the OGMP recommends that Partners use one of the following quantification methodologies: direct measurement, engineering calculation with software, or emission factor calculation

TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-05.question: What safety issue arises when measuring glycol dehydrator regenerator vents?
TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-05.answer: Even with a vent air condenser the vent can be well above 140°F (60°C), the temperature above which personnel protection is required, so Partners must confirm their tools can measure safely at those conditions.
TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-05.evidence: Because the regenerator vent with a vent air condenser can be well above 140°F (60°C), the temperature above which personnel protection is required, Partners should confirm that the tools being used can safely measure at these conditions.

TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-05.question: Which tools are recommended for measuring hot glycol dehydrator vent gases?
TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-05.answer: A vane anemometer, a hotwire anemometer and a turbine meter.
TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-05.evidence: For hot vented gases, recommended measurements tools include the following:

TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-05.question: What software is best for calculating emissions from triethylene glycol dehydrators?
TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-05.answer: GlyCalc, an inexpensive model that accurately calculates the quantity and composition of the hot vent stream, including methane, VOCs and HAPs such as benzene, toluene, ethylbenzene and xylenes.
TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-05.evidence: For triethylene glycol (TEG) systems, the best method for calculating glycol dehydrator emissions of methane as well as VOCs and HAPs (benzene, toluene, ethylbenzene, xylenes) is GlyCalc®.

TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-05.question: Why use an IR camera when preparing to measure glycol dehydrator emissions?
TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-05.answer: Viewing the whole dehydrator system with an IR leak imaging camera identifies possible fugitive leak emissions.
TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-05.evidence: Viewing the glycol dehydrator system overall with an IR leak imaging camera will identify possible fugitive leak emissions.

TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-06.question: What input data does GlyCalc need to simulate glycol dehydrator emissions?
TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-06.answer: Wet gas hydrocarbon composition, flow rate, temperature and pressure, whether a gas-driven glycol pump is used, wet and dry gas water contents, glycol flow rate, stripping gas flow rate, and flash tank temperature and pressure if present.
TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-06.evidence: gas hydrocarbon composition, wet gas flow rate, wet gas temperature and pressure, existence of a gas-driven glycol pump, wet and dry gas water contents, glycol flow rate, use of stripping gas flowrate to the regenerator, and the temperature and pressure of the flash tank, if present

TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-06.question: Is GlyCalc suitable for ethylene glycol dehydrators?
TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-06.answer: It can be used, but additional calculations with another tool such as Aspen HYSYS give a better estimate of the emitted compounds.
TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-06.evidence: For ethylene glycol systems GlyCalc can be used, however additional calculations using another tool (e.g. Aspen HYSYS) will provide better estimate of emissions compounds.

TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-06.question: What is missing from the OGMP default glycol dehydrator emission factors?
TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-06.answer: They do not include emissions from gas-assisted glycol pumps or stripping gas, which can be a significant methane source.
TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-06.evidence: do not include the emissions from gas-assisted glycol pumps or stripping gas, which can be a significant source of CH4 emissions

TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-07.question: What does Mitigation Option A for glycol dehydrators involve?
TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-07.answer: Routing the flash tank and regenerator vent gas, through added piping and valves, to beneficial use such as a low-pressure fuel gas system, a VRU or compressor suction, or to a flare.
TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-07.evidence: The possible outlets for the recovered gas include a low-pressure fuel gas system, a VRU, compressor suction, and/or combustion in a flare.

TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-07.question: How does the glycol circulation rate affect methane emissions from a dehydrator?
TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-07.answer: In normal continuous operation without stripping gas, methane emissions are directly proportional to the glycol circulation rate, so higher rates generate more emissions.
TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-07.evidence: Methane emissions from a dehydrator system are directly proportional to the glycol circulation rate in normal continuous operation when no stripping gas (natural gas) is used in the regenerator.

TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-07.question: What low-cost measure can reduce glycol dehydrator emissions?
TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-07.answer: Optimizing or reducing the glycol circulation rate and the stripping gas flow rate. Many dehydrators circulate more glycol than needed, which barely improves moisture quality but increases emissions.
TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-07.evidence: Many dehydrators are reported to be operating at a glycol circulation rate that is higher than necessary to meet gas moisture specifications, which does little to improve the gas moisture quality but increases emissions.

TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-07.question: Why is routing glycol dehydrator vent gas into a tank vapor space helpful for a VRU?
TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-07.answer: The large volume and near-atmospheric pressure of the tank vapor space dampens the variability of individual gas stream flow rates.
TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-07.evidence: The large volume and near atmospheric pressure of a tank vapor space acts to dampen variability of individual gas stream flow rates.

TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-07.question: Why should a glycol dehydrator regenerator vent have an air condenser before routing to a VRU?
TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-07.answer: The vent contains steam and non-condensable hydrocarbons; the condenser knocks out most of the steam and condensable hydrocarbons. The remaining gas is richer in VOCs and HAPs than the produced gas.
TGD5-Glycol-Dehydrators-07.evidence: Glycol dehydrator regenerator vents should have a vent air condenser to knock out most of the steam and condensable hydrocarbons when routing to a VRU.
